content.text: Enter Dogberry and Verges, with the Watch.

lines.text: Are you good men and true?
lines.plainText: Are you good men and true

lines.text: Yea, or else it were pity but they should suffer salvation, body and soul.
lines.plainText: Yea or else it were pity but they should suffer salvation body and soul

lines.text: Nay, that were a punishment too good for them, if they should have any allegiance in them, being chosen for the Prince's watch.
lines.plainText: Nay that were a punishment too good for them if they should have any allegiance in them being chosen for the Prince's watch

lines.text: Well, give them their charge, neighbour Dogberry.
lines.plainText: Well give them their charge neighbour Dogberry

lines.text: First, who think you the most desartless man to be constable?
lines.plainText: First who think you the most desartless man to be constable

lines.text: Hugh Oatcake, sir, or George Seacoal; for they can write and read.
lines.plainText: Hugh Oatcake sir or George Seacoal for they can write and read

lines.text: Come hither, neighbour Seacoal. God hath blessed you with a good name: to be a well-favoured man is the gift of Fortune; but to write and read comes by Nature.
lines.plainText: Come hither neighbour Seacoal God hath blessed you with a good name to be a wellfavoured man is the gift of Fortune but to write and read comes by Nature

lines.text: Both which, Master Constable,—
lines.plainText: Both which Master Constable

lines.text: You have: I knew it would be your answer. Well, for your favour, sir, why, give God thanks, and make no boast of it; and for your writing and reading, let that appear when there is no need of such vanity. You are thought here to be the most senseless and fit man for the constable of the watch; therefore bear you the lanthorn. This is your charge: you shall comprehend all vagrom men; you are to bid any man stand, in the Prince's name.
lines.plainText: You have I knew it would be your answer Well for your favour sir why give God thanks and make no boast of it and for your writing and reading let that appear when there is no need of such vanity You are thought here to be the most senseless and fit man for the constable of the watch therefore bear you the lanthorn This is your charge you shall comprehend all vagrom men you are to bid any man stand in the Prince's name

lines.text: How, if a' will not stand?
lines.plainText: How if a' will not stand

lines.text: Why, then, take no note of him, but let him go; and presently call the rest of the watch together, and thank God you are rid of a knave.
lines.plainText: Why then take no note of him but let him go and presently call the rest of the watch together and thank God you are rid of a knave

lines.text: If he will not stand when he is bidden, he is none of the Prince's subjects.
lines.plainText: If he will not stand when he is bidden he is none of the Prince's subjects

lines.text: True, and they are to meddle with none but the Prince's subjects. You shall also make no noise in the streets: for, for the watch to babble and to talk is most tolerable and not to be endured.
lines.plainText: True and they are to meddle with none but the Prince's subjects You shall also make no noise in the streets for for the watch to babble and to talk is most tolerable and not to be endured

lines.text: We will rather sleep than talk: we know what belongs to a watch.
lines.plainText: We will rather sleep than talk we know what belongs to a watch

lines.text: Why, you speak like an ancient and most quiet watchman, for I cannot see how sleeping should offend; only have a care that your bills be not stolen. Well, you are to call at all the alehouses, and bid those that are drunk get them to bed.
lines.plainText: Why you speak like an ancient and most quiet watchman for I cannot see how sleeping should offend only have a care that your bills be not stolen Well you are to call at all the alehouses and bid those that are drunk get them to bed

lines.text: How if they will not?
lines.plainText: How if they will not

lines.text: Why then, let them alone till they are sober: if they make you not then the better answer, you may say they are not the men you took them for.
lines.plainText: Why then let them alone till they are sober if they make you not then the better answer you may say they are not the men you took them for

lines.text: Well, sir.
lines.plainText: Well sir

lines.text: If you meet a thief, you may suspect him, by virtue of your office, to be no true man; and, for such kind of men, the less you meddle or make with them, why, the more is for your honesty.
lines.plainText: If you meet a thief you may suspect him by virtue of your office to be no true man and for such kind of men the less you meddle or make with them why the more is for your honesty

lines.text: If we know him to be a thief, shall we not lay hands on him?
lines.plainText: If we know him to be a thief shall we not lay hands on him

lines.text: Truly, by your office, you may; but I think they that touch pitch will be defiled. The most peaceable way for you, if you do take a thief, is to let him show himself what he is and steal out of your company.
lines.plainText: Truly by your office you may but I think they that touch pitch will be defiled The most peaceable way for you if you do take a thief is to let him show himself what he is and steal out of your company

lines.text: You have been always called a merciful man, partner.
lines.plainText: You have been always called a merciful man partner

lines.text: Truly, I would not hang a dog by my will, much more a man who hath any honesty in him.
lines.plainText: Truly I would not hang a dog by my will much more a man who hath any honesty in him

lines.text: If you hear a child cry in the night, you must call to the nurse and bid her still it.
lines.plainText: If you hear a child cry in the night you must call to the nurse and bid her still it

lines.text: How if the nurse be asleep and will not hear us?
lines.plainText: How if the nurse be asleep and will not hear us

lines.text: Why then, depart in peace, and let the child wake her with crying; for the ewe that will not hear her lamb when it baes, will never answer a calf when he bleats.
lines.plainText: Why then depart in peace and let the child wake her with crying for the ewe that will not hear her lamb when it baes will never answer a calf when he bleats

lines.text: 'Tis very true.
lines.plainText: 'Tis very true

lines.text: This is the end of the charge. You constable, are to present the Prince's own person: if you meet the Prince in the night, you may stay him.
lines.plainText: This is the end of the charge You constable are to present the Prince's own person if you meet the Prince in the night you may stay him

lines.text: Nay, by'r lady, that I think, a' cannot.
lines.plainText: Nay by'r lady that I think a' cannot

lines.text: Five shillings to one on't, with any man that knows the statutes, he may stay him: marry, not without the Prince be willing; for, indeed, the watch ought to offend no man, and it is an offence to stay a man against his will.
lines.plainText: Five shillings to one on't with any man that knows the statutes he may stay him marry not without the Prince be willing for indeed the watch ought to offend no man and it is an offence to stay a man against his will

lines.text: By'r lady, I think it be so.
lines.plainText: By'r lady I think it be so

lines.text: Ha, ah, ha! Well, masters, good night: an there be any matter of weight chances, call up me: keep your fellows' counsels and your own, and good night. Come, neighbour.
lines.plainText: Ha ah ha Well masters good night an there be any matter of weight chances call up me keep your fellows' counsels and your own and good night Come neighbour

lines.text: Well, masters, we hear our charge: let us go sit here upon the church bench till two, and then all to bed.
lines.plainText: Well masters we hear our charge let us go sit here upon the church bench till two and then all to bed

lines.text: One word more, honest neighbours. I pray you, watch about Signior Leonato's door; for the wedding being there tomorrow, there is a great coil tonight. Adieu; be vigitant, I beseech you.
lines.plainText: One word more honest neighbours I pray you watch about Signior Leonato's door for the wedding being there tomorrow there is a great coil tonight Adieu be vigitant I beseech you

lines.text: What, Conrade!
lines.plainText: What Conrade

lines.text: [Aside] Peace! stir not.
lines.plainText: Aside Peace stir not

lines.text: Conrade, I say!
lines.plainText: Conrade I say

lines.text: Here, man. I am at thy elbow.
lines.plainText: Here man I am at thy elbow

lines.text: Mass, and my elbow itched; I thought there would a scab follow.
lines.plainText: Mass and my elbow itched I thought there would a scab follow

lines.text: I will owe thee an answer for that; and now forward with thy tale.
lines.plainText: I will owe thee an answer for that and now forward with thy tale

lines.text: Stand thee close then under this penthouse, for it drizzles rain, and I will, like a true drunkard, utter all to thee.
lines.plainText: Stand thee close then under this penthouse for it drizzles rain and I will like a true drunkard utter all to thee

lines.text: [Aside] Some treason, masters; yet stand close.
lines.plainText: Aside Some treason masters yet stand close

lines.text: Therefore know, I have earned of Don John a thousand ducats.
lines.plainText: Therefore know I have earned of Don John a thousand ducats

lines.text: Is it possible that any villainy should be so dear?
lines.plainText: Is it possible that any villainy should be so dear

lines.text: Thou shouldst rather ask if it were possible any villainy should be so rich; for when rich villains have need of poor ones, poor ones may make what price they will.
lines.plainText: Thou shouldst rather ask if it were possible any villainy should be so rich for when rich villains have need of poor ones poor ones may make what price they will

lines.text: I wonder at it.
lines.plainText: I wonder at it

lines.text: That shows thou art unconfirmed. Thou knowest that the fashion of a doublet, or a hat, or a cloak, is nothing to a man.
lines.plainText: That shows thou art unconfirmed Thou knowest that the fashion of a doublet or a hat or a cloak is nothing to a man

lines.text: Yes, it is apparel.
lines.plainText: Yes it is apparel

lines.text: I mean, the fashion.
lines.plainText: I mean the fashion

lines.text: Yes, the fashion is the fashion.
lines.plainText: Yes the fashion is the fashion

lines.text: Tush! I may as well say the fool's the fool. But seest thou not what a deformed thief this fashion is?
lines.plainText: Tush I may as well say the fool's the fool But seest thou not what a deformed thief this fashion is

lines.text: [Aside] I know that Deformed; a' has been a vile thief this seven years; a' goes up and down like a gentleman: I remember his name.
lines.plainText: Aside I know that Deformed a' has been a vile thief this seven years a' goes up and down like a gentleman I remember his name

lines.text: Didst thou not hear somebody?
lines.plainText: Didst thou not hear somebody

lines.text: No: 'twas the vane on the house.
lines.plainText: No 'twas the vane on the house

lines.text: Seest thou not, I say, what a deformed thief this fashion is? how giddily he turns about all the hot bloods between fourteen and five-and-thirty? sometime fashioning them like Pharaoh's soldiers in the reechy painting; sometime like god Bel's priests in the old church window; sometime like the shaven Hercules in the smirched worm-eaten tapestry, where his codpiece seems as massy as his club?
lines.plainText: Seest thou not I say what a deformed thief this fashion is how giddily he turns about all the hot bloods between fourteen and fiveandthirty sometime fashioning them like Pharaoh's soldiers in the reechy painting sometime like god Bel's priests in the old church window sometime like the shaven Hercules in the smirched wormeaten tapestry where his codpiece seems as massy as his club

lines.text: All this I see, and I see that the fashion wears out more apparel than the man. But art not thou thyself giddy with the fashion too, that thou hast shifted out of thy tale into telling me of the fashion?
lines.plainText: All this I see and I see that the fashion wears out more apparel than the man But art not thou thyself giddy with the fashion too that thou hast shifted out of thy tale into telling me of the fashion

lines.text: Not so neither; but know, that I have tonight wooed Margaret, the Lady Hero's gentlewoman, by the name of Hero: she leans me out at her mistress' chamber window, bids me a thousand times good night,—I tell this tale vilely:—I should first tell thee how the Prince, Claudio, and my master, planted and placed and possessed by my master Don John, saw afar off in the orchard this amiable encounter.
lines.plainText: Not so neither but know that I have tonight wooed Margaret the Lady Hero's gentlewoman by the name of Hero she leans me out at her mistress' chamber window bids me a thousand times good nightI tell this tale vilelyI should first tell thee how the Prince Claudio and my master planted and placed and possessed by my master Don John saw afar off in the orchard this amiable encounter

lines.text: And thought they Margaret was Hero?
lines.plainText: And thought they Margaret was Hero

lines.text: Two of them did, the Prince and Claudio; but the devil my master, knew she was Margaret; and partly by his oaths, which first possessed them, partly by the dark night, which did deceive them, but chiefly by my villainy, which did confirm any slander that Don John had made, away went Claudio enraged; swore he would meet her, as he was appointed, next morning at the temple, and there, before the whole congregation, shame her with what he saw o'er night, and send her home again without a husband.
lines.plainText: Two of them did the Prince and Claudio but the devil my master knew she was Margaret and partly by his oaths which first possessed them partly by the dark night which did deceive them but chiefly by my villainy which did confirm any slander that Don John had made away went Claudio enraged swore he would meet her as he was appointed next morning at the temple and there before the whole congregation shame her with what he saw o'er night and send her home again without a husband

lines.text: We charge you in the Prince's name, stand!
lines.plainText: We charge you in the Prince's name stand

lines.text: Call up the right Master Constable. We have here recovered the most dangerous piece of lechery that ever was known in the commonwealth.
lines.plainText: Call up the right Master Constable We have here recovered the most dangerous piece of lechery that ever was known in the commonwealth

lines.text: And one Deformed is one of them: I know him, a' wears a lock.
lines.plainText: And one Deformed is one of them I know him a' wears a lock

lines.text: Masters, masters!
lines.plainText: Masters masters

lines.text: You'll be made bring Deformed forth, I warrant you.
lines.plainText: You'll be made bring Deformed forth I warrant you

lines.text: Masters,—
lines.plainText: Masters

lines.text: Never speak: we charge you let us obey you to go with us.
lines.plainText: Never speak we charge you let us obey you to go with us

lines.text: A commodity in question, I warrant you. Come, we'll obey you.
lines.plainText: A commodity in question I warrant you Come we'll obey you
